meaning: 'The man of furious face' (tū + mata + ēngā), god of war and of humankind

pronunciation.approximation: TOO-mah-tow-ENG-ah, long ū on the first syllable.
pronunciation.note: Tūmatauenga is pronounced with the long ū of the first syllable — the macron the restoration keeps — and the name means 'Tū of the furious face': tū (to stand — also the god's own name) plus mata (face) plus ēngā/anga (fury, the making of an appearance). He is the Māori war-god and the father of humankind, and his name is a face set for war.

kin.label: Māori
kin.form: Tūmatauenga — 'Tū of the furious face'; tū, 'to stand', is also the warrior's posture.

kin.label: Hawaiian twin
kin.form: Kū — Hawaiian war-god, one of the great figures of the heiau cult (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology).

kin.label: Society Islands
kin.form: Tū — war-god and, in Tahitian genealogy, the first ancestor of humankind (Henry, Ancient Tahiti).

kin.label: Modern honorific
kin.form: Ngāti Tūmatauenga — the New Zealand Army's Māori name, 'the tribe of the war-god'.

domains.title: The Standing One
domains.subtitle: War, the Angry Face, and the Taming of the Brothers
domains.lead: Tūmatauenga is the Māori god of war and of humanity's fierce inheritance: the one son of the Sky Father who stood firm when the storm-god attacked, and who then subdued his own brothers — taking their fishes, their birds, and their crops — to feed the people he had made. War, in his story, is the price of standing.

cards.name: The Mere
cards.desc: The flat greenstone club of the chief — the weapon that is also a badge of rank and a gift of state.

cards.name: The Angry Face
cards.desc: His name: the war-face (pūkana) that the haka still performs with widened eyes and out-thrust tongue.

cards.name: The Nets and Hooks
cards.desc: He snared his brother Tangaroa's fish: the arts of fishing, won by war and given to man.

cards.name: The Pa
cards.desc: The fortified hill-settlement — his architecture, crowning New Zealand's ridgelines by the thousand.

symbols.name: The taiaha
symbols.meaning: The long staff-weapon of chiefly combat — spear and club in one lineage

symbols.name: The haka
symbols.meaning: The war-dance: the body made into the angry face of the god, rehearsed before every contest of the tribe

symbols.name: The pūkana
symbols.meaning: The widened eyes and out-thrust tongue of the war-face — the literal mata of his name, worn by every performer

symbols.name: The feather cloak
symbols.meaning: The kahu huruhuru of the war-chief — honour worn on the shoulders, ransom and glory in one garment

mythology.lead: Tūmatauenga's cycle is the Polynesian account of how humanity got its arts: not by gift but by conquest — the war-god subduing his elemental brothers and distributing the spoils to his mortal children.

myths.title: The Sons of Ranginui and Papatūānuku
myths.text: In the beginning the Sky Father Ranginui and the Earth Mother Papatūānuku lay locked together in an embrace, and their children lived crushed in darkness between them. Among the sons was Tūmatauenga, fiercest of them all. When the brothers debated what to do, it was Tū who urged the final solution — kill the parents and have done. The others recoiled at the thought of slaying their own father and mother, and the gentler counsel of Tāne prevailed: the parents would be forced apart, not slain (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, the legend of the children of Rangi and Papa). Rongo, Tangaroa, Haumia, and Tū himself tried to push the parents and failed; then Tāne set his head on the earth, his feet against the sky, and tore the parents open. Light came into the world — and Tāwhirimātea, who had loved the darkness, went to war over it. The myth is exact about its genealogy of war: strife is not an intruder into creation but a sibling of the light itself, born the moment separation was chosen.

myths.title: The One Who Stood
myths.text: Tāwhirimātea, god of winds and storms, had opposed the separation of his parents, and now he took war to his brothers in revenge, riding the weapon-winds of his storm-army. Tangaroa fled to the sea; Tāne withdrew into the forests; Rongo and Haumia thrust themselves into the earth — but Tūmatauenga alone stood fast on the open plain, unbowed under the tempest (Grey, Polynesian Mythology). When the storm at last spent itself, the standing one turned on his fleeing brothers and made their domains his own: he wove nets and took Tangaroa's fish, set snares for Tāne's birds, and dug into the earth for Rongo's kūmara and Haumia's fern-root. His name is the doctrine: tū means 'to stand'. War, in the Māori telling, is first of all a posture — the refusal to move when everything else runs — and only secondly a weapon; the whole later tradition of the haka, the pūkana, and the pa is that posture made communal.

myths.title: The Arts Won by Conquest
myths.text: By subduing his brothers, Tūmatauenga made their realms noa — common, usable — and so gave humankind its technologies: the net and hook for the sea, the snare for the forest, the digging-stick for the garden. The karakia of planting, fishing, fowling, and war all carry his name, for every tapu those arts break was broken first by him; Best and Tregear record his invocation where food is made safe to eat. The cycle thus makes the fiercest god the culture-bringer: not Tāne the gentle separator but Tū the stander, who gathered what the storm scattered and portioned it out. The distribution is the myth's second doctrine. What war wins must be handed on; the conqueror who keeps everything for himself defeats the purpose of standing, and the tribe that forgets how to feed itself has lost the spoils twice.

myths.title: The Children of Tū
myths.text: The tradition gives the war-god a family larger than any brotherhood: humankind itself. Tregear records the phrase he tamaiti nā Tū — 'a child of Tū' — as a way of naming a human being (The Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary, s.v. Tu), and the southern branches of the family tell the same descent as genealogy: in Tahiti, Tū is not only the war-god but the first ancestor, the root of the human line (Henry, Ancient Tahiti). The Māori cycles draw the moral plainly. The brothers who fled or hid left their domains to be taken; the one who stood gave humans his own nature — fierceness, endurance, and the habit of war. To be human, in this theology, is to have inherited the furious face; the arts of peace, Rongo's garden and Tangaroa's sea, are the domains of humankind's gentler uncles, conquered and kept only because their fierce brother stands guard over them.

lore.syncretism: He is one face of a Polynesian-wide god: Hawaiian Kū — the great war-god of the heiau temples — Tahitian Tū, first ancestor as well as war-god, and the Cook Islands' war deities share his name and his office, the deepest layer of pan-Polynesian religion. In New Zealand his worship ran through the war-parties and their tohunga; the nineteenth-century Māori military genius — the gunfighter pa of the New Zealand Wars — applied his standing to musket and trench, and the New Zealand Army today bears his name as its own: Ngāti Tūmatauenga, 'the tribe of the war-god.' The identification is unique in the modern world: no other ancient deity is the officially patron ancestor of a modern state's armed forces.
lore.culturalLegacy: The haka — performed by the All Blacks before every match and by the army at every farewell — is his face in modern life: the widened eyes and out-thrust tongue are the literal mata of his name. Ngāti Tūmatauenga, the army's Māori designation, makes him the only ancient god officially patron of a modern state's armed forces. His cycle — the standing against the storm, the conquest that feeds the people — remains the charter myth of Māori resilience, quoted in land-march speeches and waiata alike.
lore.extendedMeditation: Tūmatauenga is the god of standing your ground — and of what standing costs. He alone faced the storm, and so he alone could feed the people; but the myth hides nothing: his fierceness proposed killing the parents, and his victories are his brothers' defeats. He asks the hardest question of every defender: what are you standing against — and what, when you have won, will your strength feed?

lore.archaeology: New Zealand's ridgelines keep his monuments: thousands of pa — terraced, ditched, and palisaded hill-forts — from the classic period, with sites like Maungakiekie (One Tree Hill) among the largest earthworks of the Pacific. The greenstone mere and the carved taiaha of the museum collections (Te Papa's among them) are his regalia; the Auckland War Memorial Museum — itself a cenotaph to the fallen — houses the war-canoes and the martial taonga of his people. The kūmara storage-pits beside every pa tie his war-and-garden cycle into the ground itself.
lore.originalScriptNote: Te reo Māori writes him with the macron as the vowel-length it is: Tūmatauenga. The oral text is the truer scripture — the whakataukī 'Ka mate kāinga tahi, ka ora kāinga rua' and the karakia of war and planting carry his name in the living language, and the New Zealand Army's Māori name, Ngāti Tūmatauenga, writes it into the state itself.
